tip: Adjectives ending in -eux swap to -euse for a woman: courageux becomes courageuse. Same with heureux/heureuse, sérieux/sérieuse.
Il faut isn't 'he must' – it's impersonal, meaning 'it takes' or 'one needs'. Il faut du courage = courage is needed. The 'il' is a dummy, like English 'it rains'.
After a quantity word, French drops the article: un morceau de gâteau, never 'de la'. Same for un kilo de, une tasse de.
Faire plaisir à someone = to please them, literally 'to make pleasure to'. The person shows up as lui (to him/her): ce cadeau lui fait plaisir.
Colors usually agree, but two-word colors freeze: bleu marine stays invariable – des sacs bleu marine, no -s. Same with vert clair.
French can't just say 'juice' – it needs a 'some': du jus = some juice. Drop the du and it's ungrammatical, unlike English.
French drops the article for jobs: sa femme est avocate, not 'une avocate'. You only add un/une once there's a description: c'est une bonne avocate.
Ça me dit = 'that appeals to me', literally 'it says to me'. Add bien for warmth: ça me dit bien = I'm really up for it.
With aimer, use les for things in general: j'aime les films = I like movies as a whole. English drops the 'the'; French keeps it.
